components.text: Whether the cited early tradition and appearance reports are sufficiently reliable to support the historical resurrection premise.
Whether Gospel and Acts reports of varied appearances possess adequate independent historical support.
Whether early Pauline tradition and reported appearances provide sufficiently reliable historical evidence for the disciples' claimed experiences.
Whether Gospel and Acts reports of varied appearances and apostolic suffering are sufficiently independent and well supported to establish the historical case.
Whether the actual evidence supplies the extraordinary evidential strength needed to overcome a very low resurrection prior.
Whether Gospel narratives can securely support the reported character and duration of resurrection appearances.
Whether literary and mythic shaping undermines all early appearance testimony rather than specifically the Gospel narratives.
Whether Christian textual reports can be treated as sufficiently historical rather than literarily constructed evidence for resurrection appearances.
Whether narrative reports of prolonged, collective, multisensory appearances securely preserve history rather than developed literary material.
Whether evidential confirmation of resurrection is sufficient to establish the wider motion that Christianity is true and authoritative.
Whether confirming bodily resurrection would establish the wider divine identity, moral authority, and doctrinal conclusions required by Christianity.
Whether appearance evidence, even if historically successful, supplies the theological bridge from resurrection to Christianity's broader claims.
Whether willingness to suffer establishes sincere, recantable testimony to bodily resurrection rather than merely general religious commitment.
Whether apostolic suffering establishes sincere resurrection testimony by showing that recantation was available and would have prevented death.
Whether the cumulative evidential framework establishes Christianity despite independent objections to its claimed moral authority.
Whether the cumulative historical case establishes Christianity despite an independent challenge to the claimed objective moral framework.
Whether disputed Gospel details undermine the reliability of the resurrection narratives.
Whether alleged divergence among Gospel accounts, specifically the number of women at the tomb, undermines their historical reliability.
Whether John's wording fits the multiple-women tradition rather than evidencing irreconcilable or invented narrative material.
Whether interlocking incidental Gospel details provide positive reason to treat the narratives as historically grounded.
Whether the Gospel sources have internal corroborative features beyond bare canonical assertion.
Whether incidental interlocking details across Gospel narratives support historically grounded testimony rather than wholesale literary invention.
Whether the biblical sources possess internal corroborative features that raise their historical evidential value.
Whether Jesus's prior theological setting supplies a bridge from a resurrection event to his identity and Christian claims.
Whether contextual divine motivation can raise the prior probability assigned to Jesus's resurrection.
Whether Jesus should be evaluated like an arbitrary resurrected person or within a theological context capable of supplying divine motivation and significance.
Whether Jesus's theological setting can raise the prior probability assigned to divine resurrection.
Whether Hebrew-scriptural fulfillment supplies independent prior evidence rather than assuming or narratively constructing the Christian conclusion.
Whether alleged Hebrew-scriptural fulfillment supplies evidence independent of the Gospel conclusions whose probability it is meant to raise.
Whether the purported prior-raising theological evidence can legitimately function as an independent Bayesian input.
Whether a theological case for Jesus can support divine moral authority despite morally objectionable biblical provisions.
Whether a purportedly divinely endorsed scriptural framework can support moral authority despite a rule permitting severe slave beating without punishment when survival follows.
Whether Exodus imposes any legal consequence for a master's abusive bodily injury of a slave.
Whether Exodus permits abusive nonfatal beating without meaningful legal consequence for bodily injury to the enslaved person.
Whether biblical slavery regulation contains protective provisions relevant to the broader charge of morally indefensible endorsement.
Whether conquest narratives necessarily depict wholesale killing incompatible with divine moral authority.
Whether biblical conquest narratives require interpreting the commanded action as wholesale slaughter of an intact civilian population.
Whether challenged biblical moral teachings can be reconciled with the goodness and authority claimed for Christianity.
Whether the challenged biblical laws and teachings can be reconciled with perfect divine goodness and moral authority.
Whether the proposed Fall-based model genuinely explains morally significant animal suffering under a good Christian God.
Whether a retroactive Fall account genuinely explains morally significant animal suffering consistently with divine goodness.
Whether the proposed retroactive Fall model reconciles animal suffering with Christianity.
Whether the proposed retroactive Fall mechanism reconciles animal suffering with the goodness of the Christian God.
Whether rational Christian commitment depends merely on conditional stakes rather than prior evidence and experienced reasons.
Whether Christianity's conditional importance gives a distinctive reason to believe it or prioritize investigation over rival ideologies.
